name: SIGMA - DNS Lookup for a Known Public DNS-over-HTTPS Provider [cardinality threshold]
description: Elastic threshold companion for rules/sigma/net_zeek_dns_doh_non_standard.yml (issue #434, found during #428's security-auditor review). That Sigma rule matches on the observed DNS query alone — any host that can send a DNS packet can emit an arbitrary label under a real DoH provider domain (e.g. `dig <random>.quad9.net` in a loop) and produce a hit without a real DoH bootstrap ever following, a gap #428's own lookalike-registration fix does not and cannot close (a different attack shape entirely: forged emission, not lookalike registration). This rule adds the corroborating signal #434 identified as already mapped in this pipeline but never used by either DNS rule: a real client queries one, or a small handful, of these provider hostnames once per DoH-adoption event — a scripted-forgery loop instead queries MANY distinct random-looking labels under the same provider domain in a short window. Buckets DNS queries matching the parent rule's own domain list (same query — the exact `sigma convert` output for net_zeek_dns_doh_non_standard.yml, kept in sync by hand since pySigma has no cardinality target to derive this from) by source.ip and alerts when a single source queries >=10 distinct dns.question.name values within the window. Threshold picked with headroom for genuine multi-hostname legitimate traffic this rule's own falsepositives already document — a real client can legitimately hit several of these listed hostnames in one session (e.g. Quad9's dns9/dns10/dns11.quad9.net variants, plus Firefox's use-application-dns.net canary query), so a low bar would fire routinely on normal DoH-adoption traffic; 10 is comfortably above that legitimate ceiling while still well below the volume a forged-query loop would produce querying random subdomains. NOT live-verified end to end (no reachable Elasticsearch/Kibana in the environment this was authored in) — structurally validated only (tests/detections/test_threshold_rules.py: schema, Sigma pairing, lookback-containment math). Tradeoff, recorded per #434's acceptance criteria: this still cannot distinguish a real DoH bootstrap from a slow/low-volume forged-query campaign staying under the cardinality bar, and a shared NAT/proxy gateway can legitimately push many real users' distinct real lookups through one apparent source.ip into the same bucket — see false_positives below. Response-side qualification (dns.response_code/dns.answers, or zeek.conn/zeek.ssl follow-on correlation, both suggested as the other option in #434) was NOT pursued here: neither ECS field pairing was live-verified against real Zeek dns.log output for this fix, and a response-code/session-correlation qualifier is a larger, separately-testable design than a cardinality companion following this corpus's own established threshold-rule pattern (auth-win-bruteforce-source-spray.ndjson) — left as a distinct follow-up if the volume-shape signal here proves insufficient in practice.
query: event.dataset:zeek.dns AND ((dns.question.name:(cloudflare\-dns.com OR dns.google OR dns.google.com OR doh.opendns.com OR quad9.net OR doh.cleanbrowsing.org OR doh.libredns.gr OR dns.nextdns.io OR use\-application\-dns.net)) OR (dns.question.name:(*.cloudflare\-dns.com OR *.dns.google OR *.dns.google.com OR *.doh.opendns.com OR *.quad9.net OR *.doh.cleanbrowsing.org OR *.doh.libredns.gr OR *.dns.nextdns.io OR *.use\-application\-dns.net)))
author: Suburban-SOC
false_positives: A real client legitimately querying several of a single DoH provider's documented hostname variants in one session (e.g. Quad9's dns9/dns10/dns11.quad9.net) plus Firefox's use-application-dns.net canary query.
A shared NAT/proxy/campus DNS forwarder where many distinct real users' genuine DoH-adoption lookups collapse onto one apparent source.ip.
